title: FCC robot ban: Can you still purchase new products?
excerpt: Expect more banned products in the future, experts warn.
content_html:
Table of Contents

Do you know where the robots running your home — your Google Nest devices, AI-powered smart assistants, and, especially, your robovacuums — come from? Do you even care? 

Well, the American government certainly wants you to. In a sweeping order from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) two weeks ago, the Trump administration effectively banned foreign-made "robotic devices" from the U.S. market, including those helpful housekeepers. 

The ruling expands the FCC's list of restricted devices under presumed national security concerns, also known as the Covered List. Citing national security concerns, the agency blocked imports and domestic sales of internet-connected devices that navigate independently (like humanoid robots) or carry cameras and microphones (like those terrifying robo dogs). But these traits also apply to the oft-AI-powered vacuum-mop hybrids that roll around your house when you're not home — some of them can even livestream now.

Fortunately, the government won't be knocking down doors and sweeping up Roombas anytime soon — devices already in circulation can remain in homes across the country, and pre-approved robots can stay on the market. 

But it has cast uncertainty on the future of new models and the average consumer's access to them. Here's what you need to know if you're in the market for a high-tech cleaner. 

What robot brands are saying

Companies are still evaluating the potential effect of the FCC's ruling on their manufacturing processes.

Several big players in robo-vacs are headquartered outside the U.S., including Chinese brands Eufy, Roborock, and Dreame. Meanwhile, the U.S.-based iRobot, makers of the Roomba, primarily manufactures its products in China and Vietnam. Like many other consumer tech categories, most robovac companies operate manufacturing lines on foreign soil.

A handful of brands, including Shark and Narwal, have reassured American buyers that they will still be able to get their hands on the latest home cleaner tech under the new rules. In statements provided to Mashable, all but cash-strapped iRobot confirmed they would continue to sell currently available models in the U.S. as they review the new regulations. 

Vacuum leader Shark, which is also headquartered in the U.S., told Mashable it is confident it can still launch new, competitively-priced models in the future despite constraints on foreign manufacturing. "We believe we are well positioned to navigate the process," the company said. 

Mashable Light Speed

What experts advise

Industry insiders told Mashable that it's still too early to say how this ruling will impact access to robotics — and whether consumers need to act ASAP.

Most industry observers are looking to other FCC actions — including previous additions to the agency's Covered List, such as foreign drones and routers — for guidance. The FCC's approach so far has been to issue universal, blanket bans on tech deemed a cyber or national security risk. Instead of naming specific companies or brands that may pose a threat, the FCC has taken the tack of banning entire categories of products that could hypothetically pose problems. 

This means individual companies have to appeal directly to the agency and develop manufacturing frameworks that comply with the federal government's new standards to gain approval for every new product line (or even a software update). 

So far, the FCC has moved fairly quickly to approve time-limited extensions for previously approved products, particularly in the case of foreign routers. In May, the FCC extended approval for companies to issue software updates to routers until 2029, not long after issuing exemptions for two notable router companies, Netgear and Eero. Basically, your existing router can still be used for several more years before it is potentially rendered useless.

Similarly, experts explained that following the agency's ban on foreign-made drones, product access remained largely unaffected for the average buyer. However, products manufactured and sold by companies based in China have proven to be an exception, sources told Mashable. Part of wider foreign policy aims, the Trump administration has taken a hard line on Chinese imports, led primarily by the FCC and its leader, Brendan Carr.

Because conversations about select products and manufacturing plans are often happening behind the scenes with the FCC, it's unclear whether these companies are being denied outright or are even asking for access to the U.S. market, market watchers explain.

This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.

While existing market access should stay relatively the same as you see it now, the FCC ruling could still delay new product lines as companies await approval. Companies will also need to evaluate existing lines to ensure they remain in compliance. Many companies expect the FCC to continue adding to the Covered List, which may further impact what products are on the horizon. 

So to sum it up: If your robovacuum is working fine as is, no need to worry. But if you are hoping to upgrade in the future, your options may be limited. 

What Mashable thinks 

Mashable's robot experts, including senior shopping reporter and vacuum tester Leah Stodart, agree that consumers could face slim pickings in the future. But you have a lot of options currently available to you if you want to fill your house with bots.

Here's everything else you need to keep in mind while shopping for a robo vac.

Additional reporting by Leah Stodart

您知道管理您家的机器人（您的 Google Nest 设备、人工智能智能助理，尤其是扫地机器人）来自哪里吗？ 你还关心吗？

嗯，美国政府当然希望你这样做。 两周前，美国联邦通信委员会（FCC）发布了一项全面命令，特朗普政府实际上禁止外国制造的“机器人设备”进入美国市场，其中包括那些乐于助人的管家。

该裁决扩大了 FCC 出于国家安全考虑而限制使用的设备清单（也称为涵盖清单）。 该机构以国家安全为由，禁止进口和国内销售独立导航（如人形机器人）或携带摄像头和麦克风（如那些可怕的机器狗）的联网设备。 但这些特征也适用于通常由人工智能驱动的真空拖把混合动力，当你不在家时，它们会在你的房子周围滚动——其中一些现在甚至可以进行直播。

幸运的是，政府不会很快对 Roomba 进行扫荡——已经流通的设备可以留在全国各地的家庭中，预先批准的机器人可以留在市场上。

但这给新车型的未来以及普通消费者的使用带来了不确定性。 如果您正在市场上寻找高科技清洁剂，以下是您需要了解的信息。

机器人品牌怎么说

公司仍在评估联邦通信委员会的裁决对其制造流程的潜在影响。

机器人吸尘器领域的几家大型企业的总部均位于美国境外，包括中国品牌 Eufy、Roborock 和 Dreame。 与此同时，Roomba 制造商、总部位于美国的 iRobot 主要在中国和越南生产其产品。 与许多其他消费科技类别一样，大多数 robovac 公司都在外国领土上运营生产线。

包括 Shark 和 Narwal 在内的一些品牌已经向美国买家保证，根据新规定，他们仍然能够获得最新的家庭清洁技术。 在向 Mashable 提供的声明中，除了资金紧张的 iRobot 之外的所有公司都确认，他们将在审查新规定的同时继续在美国销售现有型号。

总部位于美国的吸尘器领军企业 Shark 告诉 Mashable，尽管外国制造受到限制，但它仍然有信心在未来推出新的、价格具有竞争力的型号。 该公司表示：“我们相信我们已经做好了应对这一过程的准备。”

可混搭光速

专家有何建议

业内人士告诉 Mashable，现在判断这一裁决将如何影响机器人技术的使用以及消费者是否需要尽快采取行动还为时过早。

大多数行业观察人士都在关注 FCC 的其他行动（包括之前添加到该机构涵盖列表中的内容，例如外国无人机和路由器）以获取指导。 到目前为止，联邦通信委员会的做法是对被视为网络或国家安全风险的技术发布普遍、全面的禁令。 联邦通信委员会没有点名可能构成威胁的特定公司或品牌，而是采取了禁止所有可能构成问题的产品类别的策略。

这意味着各个公司必须直接向该机构提出上诉，并开发符合联邦政府新标准的制造框架，以获得每条新产品线（甚至软件更新）的批准。

到目前为止，FCC 已经相当迅速地批准了对先前批准的产品的限时延期，特别是对于外国路由器。 今年 5 月，FCC 将公司发布路由器软件更新的批准期限延长至 2029 年，此前不久，美国联邦通信委员会 (FCC) 向两家著名路由器公司 Netgear 和 Eero 颁发了豁免。 基本上，您现有的路由器在可能变得无用之前仍然可以使用几年。

同样，专家解释说，在该机构禁止外国制造的无人机之后，普通买家的产品准入基本上没有受到影响。 然而，消息人士告诉 Mashable，事实证明，中国公司制造和销售的产品是个例外。 作为更广泛外交政策目标的一部分，特朗普政府对中国进口采取了强硬立场，主要由联邦通信委员会及其领导人布伦丹·卡尔领导。

市场观察人士解释说，由于有关特定产品和制造计划的对话通常是在幕后与 FCC 进行，因此尚不清楚这些公司是否被彻底拒绝，甚至是否正在要求进入美国市场。

虽然现有的市场准入应该与现在看到的相对相同，但联邦通信委员会的裁决仍然可能会推迟新产品线，因为公司正在等待批准。 公司还需要评估现有生产线，以确保它们保持合规。 许多公司预计 FCC 将继续增加涵盖列表，这可能会进一步影响即将推出的产品。

总结一下：如果您的机器人真空吸尘器工作正常，则无需担心。 但如果您希望将来升级，您的选择可能会受到限制。
